cells.tense: You closed something recently because it was time, not because you were angry or scared.
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing you've already let go of this year, no explaining, and let that count as finished.
cells.core:
You ended something because it was finished, not because you were in a fight with it. Most people wait until the roof comes down. You moved while it still felt like a choice, which is the harder version. What's left is an ending that didn't take anything from you it didn't need to, and that's the thing to notice.

What's in front of you now is undecided ground. You could go any direction and you can feel that. It isn't emptiness — it's the part where nothing's been picked yet, so everything's still in play. The fairness running under this is plain: you gave what you had, took what was yours, and stopped when the exchange stopped coming back. Stand there a minute this week. You'll know what's worth opening next.
cells.sheetLine: You ended what needed ending, and the ground is clear for what's next.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish so what's next can start
cells.place: the soil before anything has decided what it's going to be

cells.tense: You're living in a future where everything's already over, clearing out rooms that aren't on fire yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're itching to end and stay with it for a week — no decision, no announcement, just sit with it.
cells.core:
You keep getting out ahead of things, ending them before they've had a chance to show you what they are. It feels like freedom when you do it — cut the rope, walk out, be the one who leaves first. There's a real skill in it too, knowing when a thing has run its course instead of waiting for it to rot. You just can't always tell the difference between that and leaving early.

So nothing stays open long enough to matter, and you're the reason. You're not between chapters. You're pulling pages before they're written. What you're looking for isn't another exit. It's the feeling of being met, and that only happens if you stay long enough to be found.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've had a chance to live.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish so what's next can start
cells.place: the soil before anything has decided what it's going to be

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that closed a while back, holding it open with your shoulder.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's clearly over and make one small physical ending of it — throw it out, delete the number, return the thing — then see what moves.
cells.core:
Some part of you is staying loyal to something that's already gone. Calling it patience, or commitment, or just not the right time. But the thing itself is done. You know that somewhere, or you wouldn't be tired in this particular way. Going back to it has been easier than turning toward what hasn't happened yet, so you've kept going back.

Standing there takes work, and it's why the ground around you feels flat instead of open. Not a flaw in you. A grip that hasn't been told to let go. The way out isn't a big push. It's one small motion from what you actually feel, not what you think you're supposed to do. Direction comes from that. Not from force, and not from figuring it out.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding a finished thing open because closing it scares you more.
cells.verb: letting what's finished finish so what's next can start
cells.place: the soil before anything has decided what it's going to be

cells.tense: Something's already ending in you, and you're calling it a rough patch or a bad mood.
cells.ask: Write one sentence naming what's shifting without you, then read it out loud once — no fixing it, just hear it.
cells.core:
You've been rearranging things around yourself without noticing you're the one doing the rearranging. Routines, plans, the shape of your week — they've been quietly reorganizing while you talk about them like they happened to you. The reorganizing itself is good work. You do it the way you'd fix anything else: quietly, thoroughly, without making it a thing.

Something old is clearing out. Not a crisis, just water pulling back from the shore. And you keep describing the exposed sand as a problem. What if you didn't? Name the thing that's leaving instead of asking why the ground looks different. The structure you give everything else is yours to keep. Things make sense in your presence. They could make sense about this.
cells.sheetLine: Something is already clearing out. You keep calling it a bad month.
